title: My husband Eric was given weeks to live due to cancer. I was sitting outside the hospital devastated when a stranger approached me. She sat down and said ‘Set up a camera in his room. HE’S NOT DYING. – MP STORY

blocks.text: The doctor gave my husband, Eric, six weeks to live.Six weeks.That was all the time they believed cancer had left him.I remember staring at the doctor across his polished desk, watching his lips move while my mind refused to understand the words coming out of them.
“Stage four.”“Aggressive.”“Limited options.”“Make him comfortable.”Each phrase landed like a stone.
Eric sat beside me in a wheelchair, thin beneath his gray hospital blanket. He reached for my hand and squeezed it.
“We’ll get through this,” he whispered.But his fingers were cold.
I had been married to Eric for nineteen years.Nineteen years of birthdays, arguments, vacations, unpaid bills, inside jokes, and Sunday mornings drinking coffee on the back porch.
And now I was supposed to accept that in six weeks, I might be drinking that coffee alone.
That afternoon, I walked outside the hospital because I couldn’t breathe.

I found a bench near the parking garage and sat down beneath a dying maple tree. The air smelled like rain and car exhaust. Nurses hurried past me. Families walked through the entrance carrying flowers, balloons, and hope.
She was probably in her late fifties. She wore a long brown coat despite the warm weather, and her silver hair was pulled into a loose knot.
My grief suddenly gave way to irritation.
Because sometimes the truth is so impossible that your body doesn’t know how else to react.
“Set up the camera while he’s out of the room. Don’t tell anyone. And when you see what happens, don’t confront him.”
“The doctors said Eric has terminal cancer.”
“Please,” I begged. “If you know something about my husband, tell me.”
Before disappearing into the crowd, she said one final thing.
“Don’t trust anyone who tells you to stop asking questions.”
For the next hour, I convinced myself that she was crazy.
Someone grieving her own loss and projecting it onto mine.
By evening, I couldn’t think about anything else.
Eric was scheduled for a full-body scan the following morning. The nurse told me it could take over an hour.
The next morning, while Eric was wheeled away for his scan, I stood alone in Room 417.
A vase of flowers sat on the windowsill.
Then I did something I never imagined I would do.
I took a small motion-activated camera from my purse.
I had bought it at a store near the hospital an hour earlier.
My hands shook as I attached it behind a row of books on the shelf opposite Eric’s bed.
Not because I thought I would catch Eric doing something wrong.
Because a part of me hoped the stranger had been right.
If Eric wasn’t dying, then maybe I hadn’t lost him.
I had no idea how much worse the truth would be.
Eric returned from his scan around noon.
Maybe I had allowed a stranger to make me suspicious of the man I loved because grief had made me vulnerable.
By six o’clock that evening, I removed the memory card.
I told Eric I needed to go home and shower.
I drove home, made a cup of coffee, and sat alone at our kitchen table.
Then I inserted the memory card into my laptop.
The first few hours were exactly what I expected.
Then, at 9:17 p.m., Eric suddenly opened his eyes.
He swung his legs off the bed and stood.
Eric had needed assistance walking that morning.
He had told me his legs were becoming too weak to support him.
But on my screen, he walked across the room without hesitation.
She wore a black dress and carried a large handbag.
She threw her arms around him as if they were celebrating something.
A strong, healthy laugh I hadn’t heard in weeks.
Monica opened her handbag and pulled out a bottle.
Then he sat on the edge of the hospital bed and said the words that changed my life.
“Six more weeks of this, and we’re free.”
“You really think she’s going to sign everything?”
“She already agreed to transfer the house into my name.”
Three days earlier, Eric had asked me to meet with an attorney.
He said that because of his illness, he wanted to simplify our finances.
He had told me he didn’t want me to struggle after he was gone.
Documents Eric had told me were necessary.
“You always were good at making her feel guilty.”
I wanted to drive back to the hospital and scream in Eric’s face.
Instead, I remembered the stranger’s warning.
When you see what happens, don’t confront him.
